query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys reported to date commonly contain both solid solutions and intermetallic compounds. Induction-melted Al- and Mg-rich alloys reached densities of 2.64–2.75 g/cm3 but all had complex structures; Al20Be20Fe10Si15Ti35 combined a density of 3.91 g/cm3 with 911 HV hardness and oxidation resistance at 700 and 900 °C; compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd showed region-dependent compression, plasticity, and corrosion behavior; and reported AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys contained a primary BCC constituent together with intermetallic compounds, with x = 1.0 showing the best property combination in that series. Prior studies have emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, whereas interfacial segregation, interfacial energy, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance remain insufficiently studied. The design must retain a density below 6 g/cm3 and address performance constraints associated with the tendency of Mg and dissimilar constituent elements to form stable intermetallic compounds. Starting from an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state, what single intervention hypothesis could improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance? State the intervention, its proposed causal mechanism, quantitative or directional predictions relative to the as-processed baseline, the composition and operating or test boundaries, the prior experimental evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with explicit observations that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a controlled amount of Cr into the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy will improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance by promoting the formation of a dense oxide film and refining the grain structure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state
generation.intervention: Addition of a controlled amount of Cr
generation.conditions: Processing conditions such as selective laser melting or laser cladding, and testing conditions including high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance evaluations
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense oxide film and refinement of the grain structure
generation.mechanism: The addition of Cr causes more severe lattice distortion, opening a path for atomic diffusion and promoting the precipitation of the Laves phase, which forms a network distribution within the dendritic region, thereby improving the alloy's performance
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical properties, such as hardness and yield strength, as well as enhanced corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance
generation.baseline: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy without Cr addition
generation.boundary: Density below 6 g/cm3, and performance constraints associated with the tendency of Mg and dissimilar constituent elements to form stable intermetallic compounds
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount of Cr to be added, and the potential effects of other processing conditions on the alloy's performance

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled experiment with varying amounts of Cr addition, using techniques such as selective laser melting or laser cladding, and evaluating the alloy's performance using high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Cr does not result in improved mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance, the hypothesis is falsified

System: WVTaTiCr x (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings on 42-CrMo steel substrate. Processing: Laser cladding using a LYHS series ultra-high-speed laser-cladding machine; powder mixture of W, V, Ta, Ti, Cr (45–105 μm, 99.9% purity) ball-milled for 24 h at 300 r/min (10:1 ball-to-material ratio); laser power 1.4 kW, scanning speed 8 mm/s, spot diameter 6 mm, overlap rate 30–40%, argon protective gas. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite processing challenges, and how do its microstructure, hardness, and corrosion resistance compare to traditional superalloys and arc-melted counterparts?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition of Nb, Mo, Ta, W powders with 99.9% purity). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); parameters included hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, and a triple-pass remelting strategy (3x energy input) to achieve a linear energy density of 2.83 J/mm. Test conditions: Microstructure and composition analyzed via SEM and EDS; crystal structure via XRD (Cu target, λ = 1.54 Å); microhardness measured on XY plane; corrosion resistance evaluated via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (scanning range −0.2 V to +0.2 V) and high-voltage scanning (−1.5 to +2 V). Question: What are the temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation mechanisms of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) compared to conventionally processed alloys?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using pre-alloyed spherical powder (average diameter 27.2 µm); laser power 90 W, scan speed 600 mm/s, hatch space 80 µm, layer thickness 25 µm, volumetric energy density 75 J/mm³, 180° rotation scanning pattern, high-purity Ar atmosphere.. Test conditions: Compression tests at 25, 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 °C; initial strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; engineering strain limit 0.4; specimens preheated at 10 °C/min; MoS₂ lubricant used..
